How to chop a drum break

Gazillion Industries · September 20, 2026 · updated October 28, 2026

Four bars of drums on a 1969 B-side, six seconds long, cut because the horns needed somewhere to sit out. Nobody in that room thought they were making the most reused piece of music in the world.

To chop a drum break, isolate a section where the drums play alone, set your project tempo to the break's tempo, slice it at every transient, and map the slices across pads or keys so you can replay the pattern instead of looping it. Then trim each slice to a zero crossing or a short fade so nothing clicks, and rebuild the groove by hand. The chopping is mechanical. The rebuilding is where the beat comes from.

The short version

Find
bars where the drums play with nothing over them
Tempo
match the session to the break before you cut anything
Slice
at transients, one hit per slice
Clean
zero crossings or 2–5 ms fades at every edge
Play
map to pads and perform it, do not draw it
Keep
the bleed and the room: that is half the sound

Finding a break worth chopping

A break is the part of a record where the band drops out and the drummer keeps going. The canonical ones are canonical because they are clean, short and swung: the four bars from The Winstons' "Amen, Brother" in 1969, Clyde Stubblefield's bars on James Brown's "Funky Drummer" in 1970, the opening of The Honey Drippers' "Impeach the President" in 1973. What they have in common is exposure. No horns, no vocal, no bass, so the hits arrive with only the room behind them.

You will not always get that. When the break has bleed from the rest of the arrangement, you have two choices: filter around it, or use the bleed as texture and build the beat so the tail of a horn stab sounds deliberate. The second one usually sounds better than the first.

Why the Amen break and not another one

There are thousands of drum breaks on soul records and only one of them ended up underneath three genres. The reasons are musical and they are worth knowing if you are looking for your own.

Coleman rides a ride cymbal rather than a hi-hat, which fills the space differently: a continuous wash instead of a tight pulse, so a producer can put anything on top without fighting for room. The snare has a distinctly pitched tone, so it reads as a note as well as a hit. The recording itself has a crunch to it, the sound of a small room and a hot signal path. And the four bars are not identical, so a loop of the whole thing has internal variation built in rather than repeating one bar four times.

Who actually devised it is contested. Richard Lewis Spencer, the bandleader who held the copyright, said he directed it. Phil Tolotta, the other surviving member, said the solo was "pure GC". That disagreement has never been settled and probably cannot be.

What tempo the Amen break runs at

Sixteen beats, and the whole thing is over in about seven seconds. That gives you the tempo without looking anything up: sixteen beats divided by the length in seconds, times sixty. Or the same sum the short way, 960 divided by the seconds.

Seven seconds flat gives 960 ÷ 7.0 = 137.1 BPM. Seven and a twentieth gives 136.2. Six point nine gives 139.1, and 6.8 gives 141.2. A tenth of a second at the edge of your selection moves the answer by two BPM, which is the whole reason no two sources agree on a figure. They are not arguing about the record. They are arguing about where the four bars start and stop.

Measure your own copy rather than taking anybody’s number, including that one. Drop the file in, put the loop brace on the first hit of bar one and the first hit of the bar after, read the length in seconds, divide 960 by it. What comes back is the tempo of your transfer, and your transfer is the only one your session has to agree with.

Then accept that the figure is an average. Coleman is a man, not a clock, and the four bars drift inside themselves. If bar four runs 1% slow against an average of 137 BPM, that bar is 17.5 ms longer than the grid says: 1,750 ms stretched to 1,767. Seventeen milliseconds at the end of a phrase does not read as an error. It reads as a lean, it is most of why the loop breathes, and it is the first thing you destroy by warping every bar flat onto the grid.

How to chop a drum break

  1. Find the tempo of the break and set the session to it, so your grid means something.
  2. Cut the section you want, starting exactly on the first kick.
  3. Slice at every transient: kick, snare, hat, in that order of importance.
  4. Trim each slice so it starts at a zero crossing, or put a 2 to 5 ms fade on the front.
  5. Put a short fade on the tail of any slice that cuts off mid-ring.
  6. Map the slices to pads or keys, lowest to highest, in the order they occur.
  7. Play the pattern in by hand, then quantize lightly if at all.
  8. Duplicate the bar and change one hit so the loop does not feel like a loop.

Keep the swing you paid for

The reason those four bars still work is that a person played them slightly off a grid, and slicing them to a grid is the fastest way to throw that away. Quantize to a swung grid if you quantize at all, or leave the slices where your fingers put them and fix only the hits that are obviously late.

If the break's tempo is not your tempo, decide whether you want the pitch to move with it. Repitching the whole break drags it up or down in key and changes the character of the kit, which producers have used deliberately since sampling time was expensive. Stretching keeps the pitch and adds artifacts. Time stretching explained covers which one to reach for.

DRUGS is our free one-knob bus compressor for drums. Run the chopped break through it and the room comes up under the hits, which is the sound most people are chasing when they say a break sounds sampled.

Make it sit

A chopped break usually arrives with too much information: hi-hat wash, a room, and whatever else bled in. Take the top down before you take the low end out, add weight with compression, and layer a modern kick under the sampled one if you need the bottom to reach a phone. Layering also lets you keep the sampled kick's attack while borrowing somebody else's sub; see how to layer kicks.

If you want it dirtier rather than bigger, how to make drums sound dusty is the other direction from here.

Where it costs you

Chopping is destructive. Every slice edge is a place where the room stops abruptly, and twenty of them in a bar turns a live kit into a machine gun, which may be what you want and is usually not. Heavy quantizing does the same thing to the feel. And a famous break is famous: anyone over thirty will name it in two bars, so either flip it hard enough to be yours or accept that you are in conversation with everyone else who used it.

The feel that comes out of chopping by hand rather than to the grid is covered in how to make Dilla type beats.

Questions people ask

How do you chop a break?

Match your session tempo to the break, cut it at the first kick, slice at every transient, clean the slice edges with zero crossings or short fades, map the slices to pads, and replay the pattern by hand rather than looping the original bar.

How do I get the drums out of a song?

Look for a passage where the drums are already alone, which is the only way to get them clean. Failing that, stem separation tools can pull a drum track out of a full mix, with artifacts that get worse the busier the arrangement is. Filtering alone cannot separate instruments that overlap in frequency.

What is the most used drum break?

The four-bar break from The Winstons' "Amen, Brother", released in 1969 as a B-side, which ran through hip hop, jungle and drum and bass for decades. "Funky Drummer" and "Impeach the President" are close behind.

What DRUGS does

DRUGS is a bus compressor with one macro control, called DOSE, and it is free. Turning DOSE up makes a drum bus denser rather than louder: it reshapes a break instead of leveling it, and brings the room up underneath the hits. There is no threshold to hunt for. The release reacts to the transient in front of it, so a hit gets the shorter time and the gain recovers inside the gap where pumping would be audible.

Six seconds, cut so the horn players could rest. Still working fifty-odd years later.
